entry.title: Meta Has the Distribution, Wang Has to Build the Model

link.title: Meta Has the Distribution, Wang Has to Build the Model

entry.content:
In June 2025 Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49 percent stake in Scale AI, and the company’s founder, Alexandr Wang, came along as Meta’s first Chief AI Officer. He now runs Meta Superintelligence Labs, which brought Meta’s frontier model work together, with a smaller group called TBD Lab at the center of the push to train the next models.

Most coverage treated the deal as a talent story, and it was one, with huge pay packages and plenty of drama. I find it more useful to read it as a story about structure. Meta already owns one of the best customer relationships ever built. Billions of people open its apps every day. What it lacked, at least in the eyes of its own leadership, was a model strong enough to put in front of them. So it went out and bought the person who knew how models get made.

I should say plainly that I’m an outsider. I’ve never worked at Meta, and I’m leaning on public reporting and on what Wang himself has said in interviews. With that said, here is how I read the first year.

The Supplier Takes the Wheel

Wang built Scale AI on labeling and evaluating data, the unglamorous work that decides whether a model learns the right things. Think about where that put him. Scale sold to the labs. A supplier like that sees the whole industry’s problems without carrying any single lab’s bets, and I suspect that gave Wang a particular view of where the bottleneck sits.

The last few years of machine learning point the same way. Progress has depended less on any one clever architecture and more on data quality, post training and evaluation. Raw scale still matters, but the teams pulling ahead are the ones who can tell, quickly and honestly, whether a change made the model better. Evaluation is the closest thing a model company has to a customer in the room. It is the only voice that says no.

The open question is whether a data company’s instincts carry over to running a research lab. Those are different jobs, and Wang has done only one of them.

A Closed Door

On April 8, 2026, Meta released Muse Spark, the first model from the new lab. Meta said that over nine months the team had rebuilt its AI stack from the ground up. The surprise was that the model was closed. This is the company that made open weights the center of its AI identity with Llama.

Wang explained the decision in public. He said the model touched high risk areas during early training, particularly around biological risk, and that Meta published those findings in a preparedness report. His argument was that a model inside a product can be wrapped in mitigations, while open weights can’t be recalled once they’re out. He added that Meta is working on models it considers safe enough to open source later.

There’s a fair criticism that Meta graded its own work, since the report uses its own framework and there is no outside audit. That is true of every frontier lab right now. I would add something Wang did not say, which is that the reasoning is also convenient. Safety and control point in the same direction here, and that makes me want to look at incentives. A company with a launch date and a story to tell finds late bad news expensive. The lines that hold are the ones drawn before the training run ends, when holding them costs nothing. I can’t see from outside whether that happened here.

Open Is a Distribution Decision

The debate over open and closed weights is usually framed as philosophy. It is also a question of who controls the relationship with the user.

Releasing weights builds a developer ecosystem, gets free testing and earns goodwill, but it gives up the experience, the risk and the data that comes back. Keeping a model closed reverses all of that. Meta appears to be running both tracks, with Llama for the open community and Muse for the surfaces it controls. Muse Spark came out with only a limited private preview for developers, while the main push went through Meta’s own apps, including WhatsApp and Instagram according to some reports.

That tells me where Meta thinks its advantage lives, and it isn’t in the weights. A model sold to outsiders competes on quality and price against every other model. A model inside an app that billions of people already use competes on whether it earns a place in a habit that already exists. Meta does not have to persuade anyone to open a new app. It has to make the thing in the group chat worth keeping.

Billions of Users

Here is the tension that I think defines the whole effort. If models converge in quality, value flows to whoever owns the user, and Meta is in good shape. If they don’t, value flows to whoever has the best model, and Meta has to catch up. The company is hedged on one side only, and the lab exists to close the other.

Integration matters here. Meta can build the model and the surface together, so the model can be shaped around how people actually message, share and scroll. Someone selling models from outside can’t do that. But integration cuts both ways. A model that is merely good enough, forced through every surface, can wear down the thing that made those surfaces valuable. Distribution lets you reach people. It does not make them want what you put in front of them. I would watch retention and repeat use on these surfaces far more closely than download counts or launch day numbers.

Wartime

Reports describe TBD Lab as running in a wartime mode, with long hours and fast decisions. Critics, including some current and former employees according to the coverage, say Wang’s leadership has been frenetic and that incremental progress has sometimes been oversold. I can’t judge the internal culture from here, and some of that reporting comes from people with reasons to be sour.

Two things still stand out. The first is the seam between research and the apps. A small elite group moves quickly because it doesn’t carry the weight of a large organization. But the model still has to land in surfaces owned by people with their own roadmaps, metrics and habits,. The handoff is where good research quietly dies. I’d want to know who had the authority to say what the model needed to do before launch, and whether that person sat beside the researchers early.

The second is how progress gets described. When a team lives in a sprint that never ends, there’s pressure to call every gain a breakthrough. That is corrosive, because everyone downstream plans around the claim. Better to say what improved, by how much, on which tasks, and what is still unproven. A modest honest number holds up. A large one unravels at launch.

What the Agent Is Allowed to Do

Wang has talked about building personal superintelligence, a phrase that sounds enormous. At a Y Combinator event in 2025 he also made a smaller point I found more useful, that AI agents could make execution many times easier than it was a decade ago.

Strip the grand language away and the idea is simple. An assistant that knows you, acts for you across your apps and doesn’t make you repeat yourself is worth building. It also raises questions that no benchmark answers. What can it do without asking? What does it remember, and can you see that? What happens when it books the wrong thing? Meta can control the model. It cannot control whether people trust it, and trust is what decides whether anyone hands over real work. I think that is where the long term value will be won or lost.

The Model Is the Hard Part

So here is my view in plain terms. Meta has the part of the business that nobody can buy, which is the users. Wang has been brought in to build the part that can be bought, but only with great skill and a great deal of money, which is the model. The closed release suggests Meta wants to keep the two tied together. The bet is that a good enough model, delivered inside habits that already exist, beats a better model delivered from outside.

It’s too early to say whether that bet works, and I’d be wary of anyone who sounds sure. One year is short. The better test arrives in the next few releases, when the novelty has worn off and we can see whether people keep using what Meta built.

Sources

Reporting and statements I drew on include CNBC, Meta’s leadership page, The Next Web, Let’s Data Science and R&D World. The opinions are mine.
entry.summary: What Alexandr Wang's first year leading Meta Superintelligence Labs says about a company that owns the customers and now has to build the model that serves them.

entry.title: Anthropic’s Expensive Promise
entry.content:
On October 26 Anthropic made public a registration statement it had first handed to regulators in confidence on June 1. The document names a ticker, ANT, on the Nasdaq. It names Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as the banks leading a large group of underwriters. What it does not name is a price range or a share count, and one account says an amended version that went in on November 2 left them out as well.

A caveat before going further. I have not read every page of the filing, and the figures below come from coverage of it. As of November 6 the details are still moving.

The Ticker Is ANT

Start with what is reported. The roadshow is said to begin in the week of November 9, though that timing comes from the press and not from the company. First half revenue is reported at about $16.3 billion. Press accounts have floated a valuation somewhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, and the filing does not say that. Treat every one of those numbers as provisional until the next amendment lands.

Those are the numbers everyone is arguing about, and they are the least interesting part. A filing like this describes a machine. It tells you who controls it, what it costs to run, and who pays to use it. The valuation is somebody’s guess about the output.

My claim is simple. Anthropic is selling a promise. Its governance is what makes the promise believable, its compute bills are what make the promise expensive, and its new status as a public company is what makes the promise measurable for the first time. I will take those three pieces in order.

A Board With a Brake

Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, and it has a Long Term Benefit Trust that, according to reporting on the filing, appoints four of the seven board members. The filing describes the company’s public benefit performance as measured against qualitative standards that the board sets.

In an ordinary growth company, whoever holds the votes decides, and the people holding them want growth. Here a body that is not paid by growth chooses most of the board. The point of the design is to settle in advance who is allowed to say no. If safety concerns can delay a launch, or a lucrative customer can be turned away, that is not a cultural preference. It is a control right.

A promise is worth what it costs to break. Anyone can say they will be careful. A promise backed by a board the company cannot easily reshape is different, because the people making it have given up some of their freedom to walk it back.

There is a cost, and it is the cost of every brake. A company that can choose the slower path on purpose will sometimes lose to one that cannot. I cannot tell from coverage how the trust’s rights sit alongside those of ordinary shareholders, and I would read that section closely. The open question is whether a brake stays a brake once public investors, who are buying for growth, are in the room.

What the Filing Forces

A private company tells its story the way that flatters it. A public one has to tell it in a way that survives an audit, and that changes behavior.

Definitions come first. When revenue, usage and retention are examined line by line, loose terms stop surviving. What is an active customer? What counts as a recurring dollar? Those sound like accounting questions, but they also decide what the company pays attention to, because people manage whatever gets measured. Whoever picks the definition is picking the incentive.

Then there is time. Quarterly reporting drags attention toward whatever can be shown in ninety days. Research, evaluation tooling and safety work do not produce a clean number each quarter, which makes them the first things squeezed when a quarter looks tight. Anthropic has a structure meant to push the other way, and I would like to see how it holds when the first soft quarter arrives.

Finally, audience. The filing is written for investors, but customers read it too. An enterprise buyer deciding whether to put a model inside a regulated workflow will go through the risk factors with a pen in hand. The document is a sales document forbidden from selling, an odd and perhaps useful constraint for a company whose pitch is trustworthiness.

Every Answer Has a Price

The reporting on the filing keeps returning to the cost of compute. Training and serving frontier models takes enormous spending, and that spending sits in the middle of the unit economics.

This is where AI diverges from the software business most of us grew up with. Traditional software has a gift in its cost structure. Once the code is written, serving one more customer costs almost nothing, so the game is distribution and scale, and the winner keeps a huge margin on every additional user.

AI bends it. Every request has a price. When a customer asks a question, a bill is generated somewhere in a data center, and the answer has to be worth more than the bill. How long is the default answer? Which requests go to a large model and which to a small one? Where do rate limits sit? In software those are packaging details. Here they are the business.

It also changes how to read the revenue figure. About $16.3 billion for a half year says something about demand. It does not say how much of that demand is profitable, and the filing is where the difference should show up. I would also want to know who supplies the compute, because whoever sits upstream of a cost that large has leverage over everyone downstream.

What Customers Buy

Anthropic has built much of its identity on safety and careful behavior, and in a filing that identity becomes a set of statements the company is accountable for. That points at what large customers are actually buying.

A hospital, a bank or a government agency does not first ask which model scores highest on a benchmark. It asks what the system does when it is wrong, who is told, and how fast it can be switched off. The answers come from evaluation suites, logging, approval steps and a named person responsible after launch. When the raw capability of competing models is close, the buyer chooses whoever they believe will behave well under stress.

The three pieces fit together. Governance is the reason the trust claim can be believed. Compute is what it costs to deliver the claim at scale, since careful behavior means more checking and sometimes more refusals. Disclosure turns the claim into something that can be compared against results. Take away any one and the other two get weaker.

There is also a question of who owns the relationship. If many customers reach the models through partners and cloud providers, the partner is the one the customer calls when something goes wrong, and the partner is the one building the trust. Trust rented through someone else is worth less to the company that earned it.

The Next Amendment

I am not going to predict the pricing or the first day of trading. Several other things will tell me more.

I would read the amended filing for how revenue splits between direct customers and partners, because that shows who owns the customer. I would look at how it describes dependence on a handful of large customers and large cloud providers, since concentration decides who has leverage. I would look at what it says about governance when growth and caution disagree. And once the first earnings call arrives, I would listen for which metrics management chooses to talk about, because that choice is a strategy stated out loud.

The Promise and the Price

Stated plainly, Anthropic is a company whose product is a credible promise of careful behavior, and nearly everything in the filing either backs that promise or pays for it. The board structure backs it. The compute bill pays for it. Public reporting will test it, quarter after quarter, in front of customers who read every word.

That is a harder business than the software companies of the last twenty years, which could count on near zero marginal costs and forgive a lot of mistakes. It may also be a more durable one, if the promise holds. I cannot tell you what the stock will do. I can tell you that the way this company is built, from its board to its cost structure, will shape its next few model releases, and everyone building on those models has a stake in the result.

Sources

Reporting I drew on includes NPR, the SEC filing page, Commons, Tastytrade and BitMEX. This is commentary and not investment advice, and the opinions are mine.
entry.summary: Anthropic's public filing describes a company that sells trust, and the structure and compute bills behind that promise matter more than the valuation talk.

entry.title: Apple Chooses the Integrator
entry.content:
Apple’s stock slipped about one percent on the day the company said Tim Cook would step down and John Ternus would take over on September 1. Then it recovered. That tells you how little surprise there was. Anyone following the reporting saw it coming, and the first round of commentary read like coverage of a trade.

I’d rather ask what job the board is describing. A company picks a chief executive the way it picks where to point itself, and the pick says which problem comes next. So what does Apple think that problem is?

Four Months of Runway

The facts are simple. Cook joined Apple in 1998 and became CEO in August 2011, a few weeks before Steve Jobs died. He is now moving to executive chairman and staying on the board. Ternus, who runs hardware engineering and joined the company in 2001, takes the top job. Art Levinson, who has chaired the board for about fifteen years, becomes lead independent director on the same day.

The announcement came in April and the handover on September 1, so the gap ran roughly four months. Ternus gets a long runway and a predecessor he can call. Everyone got the same message, which is that nothing is about to break, and for a company whose value rests so heavily on being predictable, that message is part of the asset. Analysts quoted at the time said much the same thing. IDC’s Francisco Jeronimo described it as a deliberate choice for execution over radical change, and Evercore ISI didn’t expect any material shift in near term strategy.

The Operator’s Edge

Reports put Apple’s value at around $350 billion when Cook started and about $4 trillion now. You can argue about how much of that is Cook and how much is the iPhone doing what it does, but he ran one of the most complicated operations in business and ran it well. He came from supply chain, and his best work was making a huge number of moving parts arrive on time at the same price every quarter.

An operator is at his best when the category is settled. The customer is known, and the work is to produce at scale and protect the margin. That’s a real skill. It also has a limit. Operations can make a good idea cheaper and more reliable, but it can’t say what the next good idea is. Maps launched badly, and the Vision Pro has had a mixed reception at best. Execution couldn’t fill that gap.

Integration Is the Point

Here’s the way I think about why Apple exists. Most of the technology business is modular. One company makes the chip, another the device, another the software. In a modular world the money flows to whoever holds the scarce piece, or to whoever owns the customer and can make everyone else compete for the work.

Apple took the other route. It builds the hardware, the software and the experience as one thing, and it sells that one thing directly to a person. The customer doesn’t buy a chip or an operating system. They buy a phone that works. Integration costs a great deal and only pays when the whole is clearly better than the parts. When it pays, the customer gets something no assembly of parts can match, and Apple keeps the relationship and the margin.

Ternus has spent his career in the part of the company where this either works or doesn’t. A chip, a case, a battery, a sensor and a piece of software have to agree with each other before anything ships. You come to see the product as the whole assembled thing, and you learn that a weakness anywhere shows up everywhere. I don’t want to overread a résumé, since plenty of engineers make poor CEOs. But the board chose someone from the place where Apple’s reason to exist gets tested every day.

Renting the Model

AI doesn’t fit the old shape neatly. Apple introduced Siri in 2011, the same year Cook became CEO, and it hasn’t turned that early lead into a dominant AI platform. The company has since decided to lean on Google’s Gemini for a major Siri upgrade after delays. One estimate I saw puts the cost around a billion dollars a year.

My read is that this is less of an admission than it looks, and also more of a risk. A billion a year is small against a company worth around $4 trillion, and if models turn into interchangeable inputs, renting a good one is a sensible way to buy time. Apple has always bought components from other people, and what it kept was the customer. The supplier doesn’t get to speak to the person using the phone.

The risk sits in the same place. Once an assistant becomes the way people ask for things, the quality of its answers becomes the quality of the phone in the customer’s mind. Apple would be promising an experience whose most important ingredient is made by someone else. A supplier that can’t be replaced soon has leverage, and Apple can’t fully control what it can’t build.

What Silicon and Privacy Buy

This is where integration changes meaning. Once, integration meant the physical object feeling like one piece. Now it’s also about where the intelligence runs and who sees the data. When a model runs on the chip in your hand, nothing has to leave the device, and that lets Apple make a privacy promise that a company with a different business could never make with a straight face.

I’d expect that to be the center of the pitch. The model may come partly from a partner, but the chip, the privacy terms, the way the feature shows up in your day and the thousand small decisions about when the assistant should speak all stay in house. That is an integration problem, and integration is the thing Apple does better than anyone.

There’s a catch. Running on the device limits what the model can do, so some work will always go elsewhere. The seam between the local part and the borrowed part is where trust gets won or lost.

What Ternus Inherits

He inherits distribution that most companies would trade anything for, since people already carry the device and trust it with their lives. He also inherits a company built for repeatability, with a habit of shipping things when they feel finished. Those two pull against each other. The AI era rewards teams that learn from live use, and Apple’s reputation rests on the opposite habit. How Ternus settles that tension will say more than any keynote.

He also inherits a question of accountability. Someone has to answer for what the assistant says to a billion people on a bad day, and that sits with the CEO. And he inherits Cook. An executive chairman who built the company’s operating rhythm is either a great safety net or a weight on a new CEO who wants to change it. I suspect the answer depends less on the org chart than on whether the two of them disagree openly and early.

What to Watch

I won’t predict what Ternus will do, since he hasn’t had much time to do anything. Analysts expect him to push on new hardware categories, with folding phones, glasses and other AI driven devices coming up most often. I’d rather watch for smaller signals.

One is how the Siri upgrade behaves when it fails. Every assistant gets things wrong. What matters is whether it knows and recovers without making the user feel foolish. Another is how much Apple is willing to say about where its intelligence comes from, since that touches both trust and its own privacy story. The last is whether Apple lets something ship before it feels done.

The Whole Is the Product

Apple’s strength has never been any single part. It has been the decision to own the whole experience and to be the one the customer deals with. The operator made that machine run for fifteen years. The engineer is being asked to make it mean something in a world where the most important part may come from someone else.

I’m not confident how it turns out. One decision almost never explains a decade. But the choice was made in public, with time to spare, and it points at the real work. If Apple can make borrowed intelligence feel like part of one device, the integration bet holds. If it can’t, the customer will start to notice who made the best part. The next two or three product cycles will answer it.

Sources

Reporting I drew on includes The Washington Post, Al Jazeera, Sherwood News, The Next Web and Yahoo Finance. The opinions are mine.
entry.summary: Apple handed the company to a hardware engineer after an operator, and the choice shows what it thinks it is still for now that AI changes what integration means.
